text:
I watched my second child crawl for the first time today, and I’m grateful I was there to see it. I’m also grateful that I get to spend a ton of time with my kids every day.

But even with that, there are stretches where the weeks just melt into each other. You get busy, fall into routine, and suddenly realize how easy it is to waste the free time you actually have.

Seneca wrote about this nearly 2,000 years ago:

“It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it.”

“Life is long if you know how to use it.”

I think part of using it well is making sure your life doesn’t become one long blur. Doing new things. Creating memories. Giving each week something that separates it from the one before it.

We guard our money carefully, but give away our time like it is unlimited.

It isn’t.

The tragedy isn’t that life is short. It’s looking back and realizing how much of it we spent distracted, busy, or waiting to actually live.

Anyway, happy Thursday.

As fun as it is to poke at the dumber parts of this market, and players, I think it is a big mistake to let this period lull you into the camp of "It is over forever". 

It is just a matter of time.

I think about what it means when people say that a market is dead, when the market never really ran on substance from the start. It ran on vapor, so surely it can continue to find reasons to run in the future.

That, and crypto does not need to reacquire everyone from scratch. It has built an enormous dormant user base of people who have already shown an appetite for speculation and already know how to participate. 

They may be inactive, skeptical, or focused elsewhere, but a sufficiently strong opportunity can reactivate them much faster than it originally took to acquire them.

There is a lot of latent demand, and the entire narrative of the space will shift once prices are slightly higher.

At some point, when you are popular enough and have already hit enough home runs to secure your life, the rational move may be to do something less stressful that is still rewarding both mentally and financially. That does not mean the edge disappeared, or that the success was mostly luck. text:
First of all, Happy Sunday. I hope it’s a well-deserved day of rest for all of you.

I said something on stream yesterday that I think is worth repeating. If you have followed me over the last decade you have heard me use this analogy many times.

As a trader, you are basically a surfer.

Right now, for the first time in a long time, the market is full of opportunity. There are waves everywhere, and there is something for almost every type of trader.

If you have been patient and have not ground yourself up into a fine dust in the bear market, this is exactly what you have been waiting for. 

And yet right now a lot of people are spending more time watching what everyone else is doing. Who caught what. Who made how much. Who got there first. More than ever, the social trading apps are making this impossible to avoid. 

If you are new, this is going to feel overwhelming, and your own performance is probably going to feel massively underwhelming.

When you first start surfing, you probably make the mistake of going out every single day, and there is nothing wrong with that but eventually you might realize that not every day is worth paddling out.

So you get a surf cam. You start checking the swell, the wind, the tide. You learn to recognize when conditions are actually good.

Discretionary trading is not very different.

You spend years developing systems, tools, and pattern recognition so that when the conditions finally improve, you can recognize it and take advantage of it.

And probably most importantly, when the surf is firing, nobody gets to the beach and thinks, “Damn, everyone already caught all the good waves.” Because you know there is a very significant chance that there are more coming.

You don’t need to worry about how much someone else made on the last one. You don’t need to chase their wave.

Just recognize the conditions, get in the water, and focus on catching your own.

The surf is good right now.

Enjoy it.

text:
Probably an important reminded for anyone feeling FOMO right now in crypto, and anyone forcing trades right now.

I’ll start by saying I am in the camp that thinks this Bitcoin move looks more like the start of a larger trend than another short-lived bounce.

That’s great because when Bitcoin trends, the entire crypto market opens up with it. You get more continuation trades, cleaner pullbacks, stronger leaders, and eventually more rotation into other names. A huge opportunity set for all timeframes. Everyone from scalpers to swing traders will have too many opportunities to keep track of.

But as a caveat I would try to remind anyone fomoing to not confuse last week with what every week should look like from here.

The first move out of a dead market is often violent because price has to reprice quickly. After that, it is normal for things to cool off, chop sideways, pull back, and let momentum, funding, and positioning reset.

Do not confuse the speed of the first move with the speed of the entire trend.

The crazy volatility people remember from crypto bull markets usually comes later, when leverage, speculation, and participation really start building on each other.

Onchain right now might be a different story between @fomo and @Pumpfun action, but for all the big liquid stuff, it’s far different imo.

Early in a trend, things can actually be much more orderly:

Strong move → consolidation → pullback → continuation.

Crypto has been bad for long enough that people are trained to treat every move like they need to chase it before it disappears.

If the larger trend is actually changing, that is the habit you need to get rid of.

The goal is not to chase every green candle. It is to recognize that the environment may have changed, stay involved, and take advantage of the resets.

If this is a real larger trend, there should be plenty more opportunities ahead and last week would certainly not be the only one.

text:
Some rainy Saturday thoughts after a few minutes of browsing.

I think it is pretty natural for 99% of people to want to respond to people talking shit about you online.

If you come from the normal world, that is how most people are wired. Someone says something disrespectful to you in person, you probably address it. IT doesn't have to be a blow up, but never the less there is some response even if subtle body language. 

And this makes sense, is normal, justifiable and predictable imo.

There is a huge issue though once you start getting a following. The problem is that online, once your account gets big enough, the math changes, and while it should be obvious, sometimes everyone needs a reminder. 

I think this is especially the case on Twitter vs Youtube and other platforms. Twitter is text and conversation driven. You are not so much scouring your comment section for feedback as much as you are maybe responding to good questions, conversation, etc. 

If 1% of people who see your stuff think you are an dikchead, at 10k followers that is 100 people. At 300k it is 3,000 people. Your rep didn't necessarily get worse, but the absolute number of people who dislike you just grew with everything else. You could expect this naturally offline. There are always going to be people who just think you are not so great. People are weird, so many times it might not even be justified.

So, there is clearly no version of having a large audience where everyone likes you. The bigger you get, the more people there will be who disagree with you, dislike you, misunderstand you, or just think you suck. It is inevitable. 

So at some point trying to respond to all of it starts to look really weird. You stop looking like you are defending yourself and start looking like you are constantly checking what strangers think about you. This is just unhealthy period, we were never meant to know this much about how others felt, or be this exposed. 

I have been guilty of this myself before, and it is a reflex driven from living a mostly offline life where that shit just does not fly, but still, its a behavior online that needs to be avoided. I still might respond to 1 out of 50 insults, and it's often a matter of my mood in that particular moment. 

Caught me while I am hangry? Oh you are fucked fella. I might say some nasty shit.  

That being said, I have really tried to just completely ignore it, and I can see exactly how it looks with a few accounts here that constantly do it. 

There used to be this one person on fintwit I really respected, I started noticing they literally respond to all the insults, from absolute losers who just want to throw mud. Even though they were being shitty people, by responding it came across as weak and gave me the ick enough to lose a lot of respect for them. I noticed they weren't even stopping at Twitter. They were going over to Reddit and Yahoo forums trying to fight for their honor too. 

Gross stuff really.

At some point you have to put the sword down. 

Nobody's family honor is being decided in a reddit forum..

Actionable wisdom of the crowds.

You do not alwys need an expert panel or another person on TV telling you what is going to happen. Sometimes the crowd, with real money behind their view, is the better signal.

Some thoughts about Bitcoin and crypto overall. 

My timeline  seems to unanimously believe this is the bottom, and we will start ripping again in October. The more I read, the less confident I get, and I am someone who thinks this has been a better area to pick up long term exposure.

I have always had this theory, the market can be right about the price, or right about the time. Not both.

The more consensus there is around where price is going, the less confidence you should have in when it gets there, and vice versa.

Bitcoin could have bottomed already, but spend six or more months chopping sideways and destroying everyone’s patience. Or October could indeed be when volatility returns, but only after Bitcoin makes another low first. Or the bullish move could begin in September (doubt it) specifically because everyone is waiting for October etc etc.

Markets have a tendency to punish precision when precision becomes consensus.
